prompt:
Read the article below and answer each of the following questions.
[Picture: photograph of a line of climbers walking up the loose, rocky path of Croagh Patrick]
Plan to protect busy Croagh Patrick
The administrator of St Mary's Parish, Westport, has said that some weathering and erosion on the mountain is due to climatic factors. However, most of it is human-related and linked to the mountain's increased popularity as a climbing destination, attracting an estimated 100,000 climbers each year.
(i) How many people are estimated to visit Croagh Patrick each year?
(ii) Damage from weathering and erosion may lead to a limit on the number of climbers allowed on Croagh Patrick meaning fewer tourists are likely visit the area. Briefly describe one economic impact this may have on the local area.
(iii) Name and explain one process of mechanical weathering that you have studied. Use a labelled diagram to illustrate your answer.
(23 marks)
display:
Read the article and answer each of the following questions.
## Plan to protect busy Croagh Patrick
[[img: qimg/jc-geo-2022-q1b-croagh.jpg | Photograph of a line of climbers, some with walking sticks, making their way up the loose, stony path of Croagh Patrick, with green hills and a lake far below]]
The administrator of St Mary's Parish, Westport, has said that some weathering and erosion on the mountain is due to climatic factors. However, most of it is human-related and linked to the mountain's increased popularity as a climbing destination, attracting an estimated 100,000 climbers each year.
?? (i) How many people are estimated to visit Croagh Patrick each year? (3 marks)
?? (ii) Damage from weathering and erosion may lead to a limit on the number of climbers allowed on Croagh Patrick, meaning fewer tourists are likely to visit the area. Briefly describe one economic impact this may have on the local area. (6 marks)
?? (iii) Name and explain one process of mechanical weathering that you have studied. Use a labelled diagram to illustrate your answer. (14 marks)
!! For the diagram in (iii), you can describe in words what your labelled diagram would show.
marking_scheme:
(i) 100,000: 3 marks.
(ii) Impact named (3 marks) + one valid point of description (3 marks) = 6 marks. Impacts could include: loss of income for local businesses, etc.
(iii) Valid process named: 2 marks. Five valid points of explanation at 2 marks each: 10 marks. Labelled diagram: 2 marks (1 mark if there are no labels). Total 14 marks. Processes could include: freeze-thaw action (frost weathering), onion weathering (exfoliation), etc.
model_answer:
(i) About 100,000 people each year.
(ii) Loss of income for local businesses. If fewer climbers come, the cafés, pubs, B&Bs, hotels and shops in Westport and Murrisk will have fewer customers. They will make less money, and some may have to cut staff, so local people could lose their jobs.
(iii) Name of process: freeze-thaw action (frost shattering).
1. Rain water seeps into cracks (joints) in the rock during the day.
2. At night the temperature drops below 0 °C and the water freezes.
3. When water freezes into ice it expands by about 9%, which puts pressure on the sides of the crack.
4. During the day the ice melts and more water seeps further into the crack.
5. This freezing and thawing is repeated many times, so the crack gets wider and deeper until pieces of rock break off.
6. The sharp, angular pieces of rock fall to the bottom of the slope and build up as scree. This is common on Irish mountains such as Croagh Patrick, where the temperature often goes above and below 0 °C.
Labelled diagram: three boxes side by side. Box 1: water in a crack in the rock (label "water enters crack"). Box 2: the water frozen (label "ice expands by 9%, crack widens"). Box 3: pieces broken off and lying at the foot of the slope (label "rock shatters", "scree").

prompt:
Examine the article below about a multinational company moving the location of one of its factories and answer each of the following questions.
[Picture: world map with red arrows pointing to: the USA (USA based head office), Ireland (Irish factory to be closed) and Vietnam (New factory in Vietnam)]
A multinational company, whose head office is in the USA, has decided to relocate one of their factories from Ireland to Vietnam in Asia. This will result in the loss of 400 jobs in the large Irish town where the factory is currently located.
(i) Name one impact of the relocation mentioned in the article above.
(ii) State one reason why a multinational company would decide to move a factory from a developed country, like Ireland, to a developing country, like Vietnam.
(iii) How does this decision by the multinational company to move one of its factories to another country show that we live in a globalised and interconnected world?
(14 marks)
display:
Examine the article about a multinational company moving the location of one of its factories.
## Factory moving from Ireland to Vietnam
[[img: qimg/jc-geo-2022-q2c-worldmap.png | World map with red arrows labelled: USA based head office (pointing to the USA), Irish factory to be closed (pointing to Ireland), and New factory in Vietnam (pointing to Vietnam in South-East Asia)]]
A multinational company, whose head office is in the USA, has decided to relocate one of their factories from Ireland to Vietnam in Asia. This will result in the loss of 400 jobs in the large Irish town where the factory is currently located.
?? (i) Name one impact of the relocation mentioned in the article. (3 marks)
?? (ii) State one reason why a multinational company would decide to move a factory from a developed country, like Ireland, to a developing country, like Vietnam. (3 marks)
?? (iii) How does this decision by the multinational company to move one of its factories to another country show that we live in a globalised and interconnected world? (8 marks)
marking_scheme:
(i) Loss of jobs: 3 marks. The answer must be about job losses.
(ii) Valid statement: 3 marks.
(iii) Banded marking, 0, 2, 5 or 8 marks only. Poor (2): little detail, no real understanding of globalisation. Good (5): some detail but does not show how the decision shows a globalised, interconnected world. Excellent (8): shows understanding of globalisation; may explain one way in detail or list several ways. One well-developed reason (e.g. transport, the internet) can get full marks.
model_answer:
(i) 400 people will lose their jobs in the Irish town.
(ii) Wages are much lower in Vietnam than in Ireland, so the company's costs will be lower and its profits higher.
(iii) The company is run from a head office in the USA, but it makes its products in factories in other continents. A decision made by managers in America changes the lives of 400 workers in Ireland and creates new jobs in Vietnam. This shows that countries are now linked together. Modern communications such as the internet, email and video calls let the head office control factories anywhere in the world. Cheap, fast transport such as container ships and air freight means goods made in Vietnam can easily be sold in Europe and America. Money, jobs and goods move freely between countries, so what happens in one place affects people on the other side of the world. This is globalisation.

display:

## Aid Project in South Sudan
When the aid project started in 2016, there were no schools. Since then, the community has built new school buildings and parents are strongly involved in their children's education through Parent-Teacher Associations.
A total of 130 teachers received training with the project, and more than 7,000 pupils can access learning spaces and materials.
?? (i) How many teachers were trained as part of this aid project? (3 marks)

model_answer:

prompt:
(i) Name one river that you have studied.
(ii) List two features that are formed by the process of river deposition.
(iii) Explain how the process of deposition forms one river feature that you have studied. Use a labelled diagram(s) in your answer.
(21 marks)
display:
?? (i) Name one river that you have studied. (3 marks)
?? (ii) List two features that are formed by the process of river deposition. (6 marks)
?? (iii) Explain how the process of deposition forms one river feature that you have studied. Use a labelled diagram(s) in your answer. (12 marks)
!! For the diagram in (iii), you can describe in words what your labelled diagram would show.
marking_scheme:
(i) Any valid river: 3 marks.
(ii) Any two features formed by deposition at 3 marks each (6). Features could include: delta, levee, floodplain, meander, ox-bow lake, etc.
(iii) Explanation with five valid points at 2 marks each (10) + labelled diagram 2 marks (1 mark if no labels). VP2 x 5 + Dg2 = 12 marks.
model_answer:
(i) The River Shannon.
(ii) 1. A floodplain. 2. Levees (also correct: a delta).
(iii) Levees.
1. In the lower course the river is slow-moving and carries a large load of fine material called alluvium.
2. After heavy rain the river floods and spreads out over the flat land on either side of it (the floodplain).
3. When the water leaves the channel it suddenly slows down because of friction with the land, so it loses energy.
4. It drops (deposits) the heaviest and largest material first, right beside the river bank.
5. Finer material is carried further and spread over the floodplain.
6. After many floods the material beside the banks builds up into raised natural embankments called levees, which run along both sides of the river, as on the lower Shannon.
Labelled diagram: a cross-section of a river valley showing the river channel in the middle, raised banks on each side labelled "levee (coarse alluvium)", flat land on each side labelled "floodplain (fine alluvium)", and a dotted line above labelled "flood water level".

(25 marks)
display:
?? (i) Which of the following terms best describes a volcano that has not erupted in a long time but may erupt again: active volcano, dormant volcano or extinct volcano? (3 marks)
?? (ii) Using the terms vent, magma chamber, crater, layers of ash and rock, and lava, explain how a volcano is formed. Use a labelled diagram(s) to support your answer. (14 marks)
?? (iii) Using an example that you have studied, discuss one impact of volcanic activity. (8 marks)
!! For the diagram in (ii), you can describe in words what your labelled diagram would show.
marking_scheme:
(i) Dormant volcano: 3 marks.
(ii) Explanation with six valid points at 2 marks each (12) + labelled diagram 2 marks (1 mark if no labels) = 14 marks.
(iii) Impact named (2 marks) + two valid points of discussion (2 + 2) + example (2 marks) = 8 marks. Impacts could include: geothermal energy, increased fertility of soils, destruction of property, etc. Examples can be specific volcanoes or places, e.g. Mt Etna, Iceland, Hawaii, Mt St Helens.
model_answer:
(i) Dormant volcano.
(ii) 1. Volcanoes usually form at plate boundaries, where plates separate or collide.
2. Deep under the surface, rock melts into magma, which collects in a magma chamber.
3. Magma is lighter than the solid rock around it, so pressure builds up and forces it upwards through a crack in the crust called the vent.
4. When the magma reaches the surface, it erupts and is called lava. Ash, gas and rock are also thrown out.
5. The lava and ash cool and harden around the vent. With each eruption new layers of ash and rock (lava) build up, one on top of another, forming a cone-shaped mountain.
6. At the top of the volcano is a bowl-shaped hollow called the crater, where the vent reaches the surface.
Labelled diagram: a cross-section of a cone-shaped mountain showing the magma chamber at the bottom, a pipe (vent) leading up through the centre, the crater at the top with lava flowing down the sides, and the inside of the cone drawn as alternate layers labelled "layers of ash and rock".
(iii) Disruption to air travel, Eyjafjallajökull, Iceland (2010). In April 2010 this volcano erupted under a glacier and sent a huge cloud of fine ash high into the sky. The ash was blown south-east over Ireland and Europe. Volcanic ash can damage aircraft engines, so most of European airspace, including Ireland's, was closed for about six days. About 100,000 flights were cancelled and millions of passengers were stranded, and airlines lost huge amounts of money.

marking_scheme:

model_answer:
Location: Rosslare Strand, Co. Wexford.
Natural processes: coastal erosion by waves and longshore drift.
At Rosslare, storm waves wear away the soft sand and clay coast, and longshore drift carries the sand away along the shore. Some houses near the edge are in danger.
To control this, the council built groynes: low walls of wood or rock built out into the sea at right angles to the beach. They trap the sand being carried by longshore drift, so the beach builds up and protects the land behind it.
Rock armour (large boulders) was placed at the bottom of the dunes and cliffs. The boulders absorb the energy of the waves, so less erosion happens behind them.
These defences have slowed the erosion at Rosslare. However, they are expensive, and because groynes trap sand, beaches further along the coast get less sand and can erode faster.

prompt:
(b) Explain how either the processes of river erosion or the processes of glacial erosion change the shape of the landscape.
(10 marks)
marking_scheme: Explanation with five valid points, 2 marks each (10). The emphasis is on how the processes shape the landscape.
model_answer:
River erosion:
Hydraulic action: the force of the moving water hits the bed and banks and breaks off loose material.
Abrasion: the river throws stones and sand against its bed and banks, wearing them away like sandpaper.
Attrition: the stones carried by the river knock against each other and become smaller and rounder.
Solution: the water dissolves some rocks, such as limestone.
In the youthful stage the river erodes downwards (vertical erosion), cutting a steep V-shaped valley into the land.
Where hard rock lies on top of soft rock, the soft rock is eroded faster, so the river forms a waterfall, which slowly retreats upstream and leaves a gorge.
In the mature stage the river erodes sideways (lateral erosion) on the outside of bends, so the meanders get bigger and the valley gets wider.

model_answer:

During the Ice Age, snow gathered in a hollow on the side of a mountain, usually facing north where it was shadier, and was pressed into ice.
Freeze-thaw action loosened rock on the back wall, and as the ice moved, plucking tore out pieces of rock, making the back wall steep.
Rocks frozen into the bottom of the ice scraped the floor of the hollow by abrasion, making it deeper.
At the front, the ice was thinner and eroded less, so a raised lip was left.
When the ice melted, water filled the hollow to form a corrie lake (a tarn), such as Coumshingaun in Co. Waterford.

model_answer:
(i) Hurricane Katrina (2005).
(ii) New Orleans, USA.
(iii) Hurricanes form over warm tropical seas where the water is at least 27 °C, in late summer.
The warm, moist air rises quickly, creating an area of very low pressure. As it rises it cools and condenses, forming huge cumulonimbus clouds and releasing heat, which makes the air rise even faster.
Air rushes in from all sides to replace it, and the spin of the earth (the Coriolis effect) makes it spiral around the centre. In the middle a calm, clear "eye" forms, surrounded by the eye wall with the strongest winds.
Katrina grew over the warm Gulf of Mexico and hit New Orleans with winds of over 200 km/h and a storm surge that broke the levees.

(12 marks)
display: ?? (b) Explain how the processes of erosion form one coastal feature that you have studied. Describe the labelled diagram you would draw (for example, label the headland, crack, cave, arch and stack). (12 marks)
marking_scheme: Labelled diagram: 2 marks. Explanation: five valid points of explanation, 2 marks each (10). Total 12. The diagram must be labelled to get its marks. Points must explain how erosion processes (hydraulic action, compression, abrasion, solution) form the feature (e.g. sea cave, sea arch, sea stack, cliff, bay and headland).
model_answer:
Feature: sea arch (and sea stack).
1. A sea arch forms on a headland where the rock has a line of weakness, such as a crack or fault.
2. Waves attack the crack by hydraulic action: the force of the water is pushed into the crack, and air trapped inside is squeezed (compression). When the wave pulls back, the air expands with great force and the crack gets wider.
3. Abrasion also takes place: the waves throw sand and stones against the rock, wearing it away, so the crack gets bigger and becomes a sea cave.
4. Caves often form on both sides of the headland. Erosion continues until the two caves meet back to back and break through, forming a sea arch.
5. Over time the sea keeps eroding the base of the arch, and weathering attacks the roof. Eventually the roof collapses, leaving a pillar of rock standing on its own in the sea. This is a sea stack (for example, Dún Briste at Downpatrick Head, Co. Mayo).
Diagram: a headland drawn in stages, labelled: crack/fault, waves, sea cave, sea arch, collapsed roof, sea stack.

model_answer:
Named example: Basalt.
Description:
1. Basalt is an igneous rock, formed from magma (molten rock) that has cooled and hardened.
2. It forms when lava pours out onto the earth's surface during a volcanic eruption (it is an extrusive rock).
3. Because it is on the surface, the lava cools very quickly, so only very small crystals have time to form. This makes basalt fine-grained and dark grey or black.
4. Sometimes, as thick lava cools slowly and shrinks, it cracks into six-sided columns. An Irish example is the Giant's Causeway in Co. Antrim, formed about 60 million years ago.

display: ?? (b) Explain the formation of one underground feature found in a karst landscape. Describe the labelled diagram you would draw to support your answer (for example, label the cave roof, dripping water, calcite and the feature). (10 marks)
marking_scheme: Labelled diagram: 2 marks. Explanation: four valid points, 2 marks each (8). Total 10. No marks for surface features (e.g. limestone pavement, swallow hole); the focus is on how the feature forms. The diagram must be labelled to get marks.
model_answer:
Feature: stalactite (for example in Aillwee Cave, the Burren).
1. Rainwater mixed with carbon dioxide forms weak carbonic acid. As it seeps down through the joints in the limestone, it dissolves calcium carbonate from the rock (carbonation).
2. When this water reaches the roof of an underground cave, it hangs there as a drop.
3. As the drop hangs, some of the water evaporates and carbon dioxide is released, so a tiny amount of calcite (calcium carbonate) is left behind on the cave roof.
4. Over thousands of years, drop after drop adds more calcite, and a long thin "icicle" of rock grows down from the roof. This is a stalactite. (If it joins a stalagmite growing up from the floor, they form a pillar.)
Diagram: a cross-section of a cave, labelled: limestone, joints, cave roof, water drip, stalactite hanging from the roof, stalagmite on the floor, pillar.

display:

[[img: qimg/jc-hec-2022-q11f-online.jpg | A hand holding a bank card over a laptop keyboard, with colourful shopping app icons floating above the screen]]

marking_scheme:
Name of law: 2 marks, graded 2/1/0. Description: 2 points x 5 marks (10), graded 5/2/0.
Accepted laws and points:
Sale of Goods and Supply of Services Act 1980: goods must be of merchantable quality, fit for purpose, as described, the same as any sample shown; right to redress.
Consumer Protection Act 2007: protects against false or misleading claims about goods, services or prices, including the price, previous price or recommended retail price.
Electronic Commerce Act 2000: electronic signatures, contracts and documents have the same recognition as written ones.
Consumer Rights Directive 2014: clear information before you buy; refund if goods are not delivered; return goods if you change your mind or they are faulty; cancel a service or digital purchase; cooling-off period.
model_answer:
Name of law: the Consumer Rights Directive 2014.
How it protects the consumer: 1. The seller must give clear information before you buy, such as the full price including delivery and the seller's address.
2. You have a 14-day cooling-off period: you can cancel the order and return the goods within 14 days even if nothing is wrong with them, and get a full refund. If the goods are never delivered, you are entitled to your money back.

?? (b)(i) Analyse four different hygiene guidelines that should be followed to reduce the risk of food poisoning. (16 marks)
[[img: qimg/jc-hec-2024-q11b-people.jpg | A large group of smiling people of all ages, from small children to older adults]]

marking_scheme:
(i) Four analysed guidelines, 4 marks each (16), graded 4/2/0. Accepted: personal hygiene (wash hands, cover cuts, tie back hair, wear gloves); kitchen hygiene (clean and disinfect floors, surfaces and bins; wash kitchen cloths regularly); store foods at the correct temperature (cold food in the fridge, hot food above the danger zone); cook food thoroughly (no pink, use a food thermometer); follow rules for defrosting and cooking frozen food; protect food from insects, flies and pets.
(ii) Two groups, 3 marks each (6): pregnant women; older people; infants and small children; people with a weakened immune system. Reason: 2 marks: less able to fight off a food poisoning infection; likely to become more seriously ill; food poisoning bacteria can harm an unborn baby.
model_answer:
(i) 1. Wash your hands with hot soapy water before handling food and after using the toilet or touching raw meat, because hands easily carry bacteria onto food.
2. Keep the kitchen clean: wipe and disinfect work surfaces and wash dishcloths often, as bacteria multiply on dirty, damp surfaces.
3. Store food at the right temperature: keep high-risk foods in the fridge (0-5°C), because bacteria grow fastest in the danger zone (5-63°C).
4. Cook food thoroughly, especially chicken and minced meat, until it is piping hot with no pink, to kill bacteria. A food thermometer should read at least 75°C.
(ii) 1. Older people. 2. Pregnant women. (Babies and young children are also correct.)
Why: their immune systems are weaker, so they cannot fight off the bacteria as easily and they become more seriously ill. In pregnant women, bacteria such as Listeria can also harm the unborn baby.

[[img: qimg/jc-hec-2024-q12b-menu.jpg | A menu scroll with photos of a fish pie with a potato topping, carrots and broccoli, and a fruit crumble with a jug of custard]]
Potato topped cod and salmon pie with carrots and broccoli
Apple and berry wholegrain crumble with custard
?? (b)(i) Analyse this menu and explain how the menu meets the nutritional and dietary needs of an older person. Give four different points. (16 marks)
marking_scheme:
(a) Three discussed points, 5 marks each (15), graded 5/2/0: one on healthy diet, one on exercise, one on spending time with friends and family.
(b)(i) Four points related to the menu and correctly explained, 4 marks each (16), graded 4/2/0. Expect one nutritional point, one dietary point and any two others.
model_answer:
(a) Healthy diet: a balanced diet with plenty of calcium and vitamin D (milk, cheese, oily fish) keeps bones strong and helps prevent osteoporosis, while fibre prevents constipation and less salt and saturated fat protects the heart.
Exercise: regular gentle exercise, like walking or swimming, keeps the heart, muscles and joints healthy, helps control weight and improves balance, which reduces the risk of falls.
Spending time with friends and family: it prevents loneliness and isolation, keeps the mind active and improves mood and mental health.
(b)(i) 1. The cod and salmon give protein to repair body cells. Salmon is an oily fish, so it also gives omega-3 fatty acids, which protect the heart, and vitamin D, which helps the body absorb calcium for strong bones.
2. The custard is made with milk, which gives calcium for strong bones and teeth and helps prevent osteoporosis, a common problem in older people.
3. The wholegrain crumble topping, the fruit and the vegetables give fibre, which prevents constipation, a common problem in older people. The carrots, broccoli and berries also give vitamins A and C.
4. The meal is soft and easy to chew and digest (the potato topping, fish and crumble), which suits older people who may have dentures or poor teeth. It is also low in salt and fried food, which helps protect against high blood pressure.

(16 marks)

[[img: qimg/jc-hec-2024-q13c-diabetes.jpg | Blue map of Ireland and Britain with an orange circle around Ireland]]
?? (c)(i) Outline why some people may be at risk of developing diabetes. Give two points. (8 marks)
?? (c)(ii) Describe two guidelines to follow when planning meals for a person with diabetes. (8 marks)
marking_scheme:
(i) Two reasons, 4 marks each (8), graded 4/2/0. Accepted: being obese or overweight; the body cannot use the insulin it makes correctly; pregnancy (gestational diabetes); where excess body fat is stored; diet; the body makes no insulin or not enough; genetic reasons.
(ii) Two described guidelines, 4 marks each (8), graded 4/2/0. Accepted: eat a healthy balanced diet; eat regular meals and do not skip meals; manage or avoid sugary foods; choose high-fibre carbohydrate foods; choose low-GI carbohydrates; avoid high-fat foods; use low-fat cooking methods; avoid high-salt foods.
model_answer:
(i) 1. Being overweight or obese, especially carrying extra fat around the waist, makes the body less able to use insulin properly (type 2 diabetes). An unhealthy diet high in sugar and fat and little exercise add to this.
2. Genetics: people with a parent, brother or sister with diabetes are more at risk.
(ii) 1. Eat regular meals at the same times each day and never skip meals, so the blood sugar level stays steady.
2. Choose high-fibre, low-GI carbohydrates, like porridge, wholemeal bread and brown rice, and cut down on sugary foods and drinks, because they release sugar slowly instead of causing a sudden rise in blood sugar.

model_answer:
1. Nutrition information: a person with diabetes can check the sugar content per 100 g and choose the product with the least sugar.

Words to choose from: credit, want, food, saving, goals, net income
- Management means using resources to achieve ______.
- A budget is a plan for spending and ______ money.
- An example of an item of essential expenditure is ______.
- Buying on ______ means "buy now pay later".

- A ______ is something that we can live without e.g. the latest smartphone.
?? (a) Choose the correct word from the list to complete each sentence. (12 marks)
marking_scheme:
6 words correctly chosen @ 2 marks each (12), graded 2 or 0.
goals; saving; food; credit; net income; want.
model_answer:
Management means using resources to achieve goals.
A budget is a plan for spending and saving money.
An example of an item of essential expenditure is food.
Buying on credit means "buy now pay later".
Our take-home pay, after tax is deducted, is called net income.
A want is something that we can live without e.g. the latest smartphone.

marking_scheme:
(a)(i) 2 nutrients @ 3 marks (graded 3:0) + 2 functions @ 3 marks (graded 3:0) = 12. Nutrients: vitamins A, B, C, D, E, K; minerals (iron, calcium, etc.); carbohydrate (sugar, starch, fibre); protein; fat. Accept any correct function.
(a)(ii) 3 ways described @ 4 marks each (12), graded 4:2:0. Accepted: eat raw if possible; use a sharp knife to avoid damaging cells; avoid peeling or peel thinly (keeps fibre and vitamins); do not steep in water (water-soluble vitamins leach out); do not prepare too far in advance; cook for the shortest time; use a small amount of water; cook with the lid on; avoid overcooking; avoid reheating, etc.
(b)(i) Explanation @ 5 marks, graded 5:3:0: found on foods with a longer shelf life (e.g. breakfast cereals); these are low risk, so the date is about quality, not safety; food past its best-before date may be safe to eat if it looks and smells fine, but the quality may be lower.
(b)(ii) 3 points @ 5 marks each (15), graded 5:3:0. Accepted: bright, even colour; no dark spots or mould; no bruises, dents or damaged skin; not wilting; firm to touch, not rubbery, etc.
model_answer:
(a)(i)

Nutrient 2: Fibre (NSP). Function: it helps food move through the intestines and prevents constipation.
(a)(ii)
1. Prepare vegetables just before cooking and do not leave them steeping in water, because vitamin C is water-soluble and dissolves out into the water.
2. Peel thinly or not at all, because many vitamins and minerals are just under the skin, and use a sharp knife so cells are not damaged.
3. Cook in a small amount of boiling water with the lid on for the shortest time (or steam them), and serve straight away. Overcooking and keeping food warm destroy vitamin C.
(b)(i) A best-before date is about quality, not safety. It is found on foods with a longer shelf life, such as cereals and tinned food. After the date the food may lose some flavour or texture, but it is usually still safe to eat if it looks and smells fine.
(b)(ii)
1. Colour: the vegetable should have a bright, even colour, for example green broccoli with no yellowing.
2. Skin: there should be no mould, dark spots, bruises, dents or damaged skin.
3. Texture: it should be firm and crisp to touch, not soft, rubbery or wilted, for example carrots should snap and lettuce leaves should be crisp.

?? Explain the term cross-contamination.

marking_scheme:

Ann and Paul Green have two children, Siobhán (12) and John (14). Ann is a stay at home parent and she cares for her elderly mother who has osteoporosis.

Lunch Menu

display:
Ann and Paul Green have two children, Siobhán (12) and John (14). Ann is a stay at home parent and she cares for her elderly mother who has osteoporosis.
Ann's mother has osteoporosis (a diet-related disease).
?? (c)(i) What is osteoporosis? (5 marks)
?? (c)(ii) Outline two guidelines that should be followed to reduce the risk of developing osteoporosis. (8 marks)
?? (d)(i) Design a lunch menu with a drink suitable for a person who has osteoporosis. Write it out as a menu. (14 marks)
?? (d)(ii) Describe three meal planning guidelines you followed when planning the lunch menu. (15 marks)
marking_scheme:
(c)(i) 1 point fully explained @ 5 marks, graded 5:3:0: a brittle bone disease where bones lose calcium and become weak and break easily; caused by a lack of calcium, vitamin D or phosphorus, etc.
(c)(ii) 2 guidelines @ 4 marks each (8), graded 4:2:1:0: increase intake of calcium, vitamin D and phosphorus foods from an early age (dairy products); weight-bearing exercise; avoid alcohol, etc.
(d)(i) Menu (14): 2 courses balanced using the food pyramid @ 4 marks each (8), graded 4:2:0; a suitable healthy drink 4 marks (graded 4:2:0); menu format 2 marks.
(d)(ii) 3 guidelines @ 5 marks each (15), graded 5:3:0. One must relate directly to nutrition for osteoporosis (calcium, vitamin D, phosphorus for healthy bones). Others: iron for healthy blood; carbohydrate for energy; protein for growth and repair; variety of colour and flavour; avoid overeating if not mobile; easy to eat; suitable drinks (milk or water); time; avoid overly processed foods; cost; using foods in season, etc.
model_answer:
(c)(i) Osteoporosis is a brittle bone disease. The bones lose calcium and become thin, weak and porous, so they break easily, especially the hips, wrists and spine. It is linked to a lack of calcium and vitamin D in the diet.
(c)(ii)
1. Eat plenty of calcium and vitamin D foods from a young age, such as milk, cheese, yoghurt, oily fish and fortified cereals, to build strong bones.
2. Do regular weight-bearing exercise, such as walking, dancing or running, which strengthens bones. Avoid smoking and too much alcohol.
(d)(i) Lunch Menu
Starter: Creamy vegetable soup made with milk, with a wholemeal brown bread roll
Main course: Tinned salmon and cheese salad sandwich on wholemeal bread with mixed leaves and tomato
Drink: A glass of low-fat milk
(d)(ii)
1. Include calcium and vitamin D for bones: the milk in the soup and drink, the cheese, and the tinned salmon (with its soft bones) give calcium, and salmon gives vitamin D, which helps the body absorb calcium. This is important for someone with osteoporosis.
2. Follow the food pyramid for a balanced meal: wholemeal bread for carbohydrates and fibre (energy and to prevent constipation), salad and vegetables for vitamins and minerals, and salmon and cheese for protein.
3. Make it easy to eat: an elderly person may have weaker hands or teeth, so I chose soft foods like soup and a sandwich that are easy to chew, with little preparation needed.

marking_scheme:
(c)(i) 1 point @ 4 marks, graded 4:2:0: the process of adding decorative details to fabric to improve its appearance and make it more visually interesting, e.g. embroidery, tie-dye, beading, ribbon work, appliqué, fabric painting, etc.
(c)(ii) 2 points @ 4 marks each (8), graded 4:2:0. Washing: low temperature/cool wash, hand wash. Drying: line dry, avoid the tumble dryer. Ironing: on the wrong side, cover with a towel. Storing: inside out, fold neatly, etc.
(d) Sketch of 2 different embellishments on the jacket @ 3 marks each (6), graded 3:1:0. Description of how to apply each @ 4 marks each (8), graded 4:2:0.
model_answer:
(c)(i) Fabric embellishment means adding decoration to fabric to make it look more attractive and interesting, for example with embroidery, appliqué, beading, fabric paint or tie-dye.
(c)(ii)
1. Wash it inside out by hand or on a cool, gentle cycle, so the stitches, beads or paint are not damaged, and dry it on a line, not in the tumble dryer.
2. Iron it on the wrong side, with a towel underneath the decorated area, and store it folded neatly or on a hanger so the decoration does not get crushed or snagged.
(d)
Embellishment 1: Appliqué on the back of the jacket. I would cut a large star shape from a contrasting fabric, pin and tack it in the centre of the back panel, then sew around the edge with a close zig-zag (satin) stitch on the sewing machine to stop it fraying. Then I would remove the tacking.
Embellishment 2: Machine embroidery on the collar and pocket edges. I would draw the design (my initials and a small flower) with tailor's chalk, put the area in an embroidery hoop, and sew over the lines with a decorative stitch in bright thread (or use a computerised embroidery machine).
